title: Gur
html:
The Gur are a nomadic people in Baldur's Gate

“
Your friend has just heard the rumours of my people. That we steal chickens, curse your crops, seduce your daughters... I wish I had half the power settled folk think my people possess. Alas, I am a simple wanderer.
„
— Gandrel unfazed by Astarion's remarks

Involvement

The party can meet one member of the Gur,  Gandrel near  Auntie Ethel's gnarled teahose in Act One. Later in Act Three the party can meet some Gur in their in Rivington.

 Astarion has a particularly low opinion of the Gur, calling them "duplicitous reprobates", "easy to buy and morally vacuous" and "wandering cut-throats". It is later revealed he has a personal history with the Gur[1]. The player character is given the opportunity to push back on some these remarks.[2][3][4]

Astarion reveals that he was killed by a mob of angry Gur. If the player character asks about his past with Cazador, Astarion may elaborate that they attacked because they were angry about a ruling he had made as magistrate.[5]

When the party meet Ulma, or Gandrel, in Act Three, they may acknowledge how Astarion has changed, and invite him to start righting his wrongs by promising to save the children he once abducted.

Culture

The Gur are known for monster-hunting and fortune-telling.[6]

They are said to have descended from two formerly Wychlaran maidens who were blessed by Selûne.[7]

“
Rech té i hathran roost.

Frey vald isk durovna. Frey vald isk ablast.

Im orak ne tay. Krasin ne trah!
„
— Members of the Gur, Funeral rites in the Gur language

Notes and references

  1. ↑ Astarion: "It was a mob of Gur that left me half-dead two hundred years ago. That left me begging Cazador to turn me so I could survive to take revenge."
  2. ↑ Player character: "I knew you were a jackass, but a racist? I'm shocked."
  3. ↑ Player character: "You killed him because you're bigoted against his people?"
  4. ↑ Player: "You can't hold every Gur responsible for what happened to you."
  5. ↑ Player character: "How were you turned? Did he attack you?"
    Astarion: "Not him, no. A gang of thugs attacked me, angry about a ruling that I'd handed down as magistrate."
    "They beat me to death's door when Cazador appeared. He chased them off and offered to save me. To give me eternal life."
  6. ↑ * Parallels can be drawn from the Gur to the common cultural perception of Romani and Roma people. Wizards of the Coast have previously drawn criticism for the Vistani, a similar nomadic group depicted in Curse of Strahd. Some of these criticisms were addressed and retconned with the release of Van Ritchens Guide to Ravenloft and the revamped premium edition of Curse of Strahd. ("Retcon" – short for retroactive continuity – is a literary technique where established facts in a fictional story are adjusted, ignored, or reinterpreted by new, subsequent information)
    • It is noteworthy that beyond both groups being nomadic and prone to fortune-telling and monster hunting, their storylines are also both interwoven with that of a powerful vampire. However, the Vistani are neutral to Strahd, while the Gur are actively hostile towards Cazador.
    • One of the revisions in the revamped edition was clarifying that only some Vistani were servants of the Vampire Strahd. In Baldur's Gate 3, Astarion may suggest the Gur are working for, or being manipulated by, Cazador. While it appears the Gur are not knowingly working for Cazador, the claim may not be entirely unsubstantiated: if Gandrel is allowed to capture and leave with Astarion, Astarion does end up eventually captured by Cazador.
  7. ↑  The Approachable East, Vol. 3
